ethnic_groups.name: Kalinago (Carib)
ethnic_groups.notes: Only surviving pre-Columbian Caribbean indigenous population; ~3,000 in Kalinago Territory (3,700 acres, northeast); basket weaving; canoe building; fought European colonization for 250+ years; DNA studies show mainland South American origins

country_profile.notes_unique: 'Nature Isle of the Caribbean' (365 rivers, one for every day; boiling lake; volcanic; rainforest); only island with surviving Kalinago (Carib) population; Hurricane Maria September 18, 2017 (Category 5, destroyed 90% structures, PM called 'devastation of unprecedented dimension'); Citizenship by Investment (passport sales, controversial); Roseau ('Rose Water'); Eugenia Charles (first female PM in Caribbean, supported US Grenada invasion 1983); Morne Trois Pitons (UNESCO); NOT the Dominican Republic

910.name: Kalinago (Carib) Stronghold
910.description: Dominica as the heartland of the Kalinago (Island Carib) people, who fiercely defended their territory and made Dominica the last Caribbean island to be colonized by Europeans. The mountainous volcanic terrain provided natural defenses that European powers could not easily overcome.

sub_clusters.name: Early Settlement and Arawak Peoples
sub_clusters.description: The earliest settlers of Dominica, Orthoiroid and later Arawak (Igneri) peoples from South America, who established agricultural communities on the island's river valleys and coastal areas.

sub_clusters.name: Kalinago Dominance and Warrior Culture
sub_clusters.description: The Kalinago (Caribs) migrated from South America and established Dominica as their primary stronghold in the Lesser Antilles. Their warrior culture, seafaring prowess, and the island's rugged mountainous terrain made them virtually unconquerable. The Kalinago called the island 'Wai'tu kubuli' (Tall is her body).

920.name: European Contact and Kalinago Resistance
920.description: Columbus sighted Dominica on a Sunday (hence its name) in 1493, but fierce Kalinago resistance and the island's impenetrable terrain prevented European colonization for over 150 years — making it the last major Caribbean island to be settled by Europeans.

sub_clusters.name: Columbus Sighting and Failed Colonization Attempts
sub_clusters.description: Columbus sighted the island on November 3, 1493 (a Sunday — 'Dies Dominica' in Latin, hence the name). Multiple Spanish, French, and English expeditions attempted to establish footholds but were repelled by the Kalinago. The island was officially declared a neutral territory.
key_events: Columbus sights and names Dominica on Sunday, November 3, 1493
Repeated European attempts at colonization repelled by Kalinago warriors

930.name: French-British Colonial Contest
930.description: Dominica became a contested territory between France and Britain, changing hands multiple times. French missionaries and settlers gradually encroached on Kalinago territory, while Maroon communities of escaped enslaved people established independent settlements in the mountainous interior.

sub_clusters.name: French Encroachment and Missionary Activity
sub_clusters.description: French missionaries and settlers gradually established a presence despite the island's official neutral status. French planters developed coffee and sugar estates, importing enslaved Africans, while the Kalinago were pushed into increasingly marginal territory.

sub_clusters.name: British Takeover and Maroon Wars
sub_clusters.description: Britain gained formal control of Dominica through the Treaty of Paris (1763). Communities of escaped enslaved people (Maroons) established free settlements in the mountainous interior and fought against the colonial authorities. France recaptured the island briefly (1778–1783) and attempted another invasion in 1805.

sub_clusters.name: Plantation Economy and Slavery
sub_clusters.description: The development of sugar, coffee, and cacao plantations in the river valleys, sustained by enslaved African labor. Dominica's rugged terrain limited large-scale plantation agriculture compared to flatter islands, contributing to a larger proportion of small-scale farming and a relatively larger free colored population.

940.name: Emancipation and 19th-Century Development
940.description: The abolition of slavery, emancipation in 1834, and Dominica's unique position as the only British Caribbean colony with a Black-controlled legislature in the early post-emancipation period, before crown colony rule was reimposed.

sub_clusters.name: Emancipation and the Black-Controlled Legislature
sub_clusters.description: After emancipation in 1834, Dominica became unique in the British Caribbean: by 1838 its assembly was controlled by elected members of African descent — the only colony where this occurred. This was a remarkable achievement in the post-slavery Caribbean.
key_events: Dominica's assembly controlled by elected Black members by 1838 — unique in British Caribbean

sub_clusters.name: Crown Colony Rule Reimposed
sub_clusters.description: The British authorities, alarmed by Black political power, gradually eroded Dominican self-governance and reimposed direct Crown Colony rule by 1898, stripping away the representative institutions that had allowed Black political participation.

950.name: Labour Movement and Independence
950.description: The rise of labor organizing, the banana economy, and the path to independence on November 3, 1978 — exactly 485 years after Columbus sighted the island.

sub_clusters.name: Banana Economy and Labour Movement
sub_clusters.description: Bananas replaced sugar as Dominica's primary export crop. Labour unions organized agricultural workers, and political movements demanded self-governance. The Dominica Labour Party emerged as the dominant political force.

sub_clusters.name: Independence — November 3, 1978
sub_clusters.description: Dominica became an associated state in 1967 and achieved full independence on November 3, 1978 — notably choosing to become a republic rather than retaining the British monarch as head of state. Patrick John became the first Prime Minister.

950.name: Post-Independence Political Challenges
950.description: The turbulent early years of independence, including Hurricane David's devastating impact (1979), attempted coups, political instability, and the long premiership of Dame Eugenia Charles — the Caribbean's first female Prime Minister.

sub_clusters.name: Hurricane David and Political Turmoil
sub_clusters.description: Hurricane David struck on August 29, 1979, devastating the island — destroying 80% of homes and virtually all banana crops. The disaster compounded political instability under Prime Minister Patrick John, who was removed from office.

sub_clusters.name: Dame Eugenia Charles — First Female Caribbean PM
sub_clusters.description: Dame Mary Eugenia Charles became Prime Minister in 1980, serving until 1995 — the first female head of government in the Caribbean. She was a staunch anti-communist who supported the US invasion of Grenada in 1983 and led Dominica's recovery from Hurricane David.

960.name: Contemporary Dominica
960.description: Modern Dominica confronting extreme climate vulnerability, Hurricane Maria's catastrophic impact in 2017, the preservation of Kalinago Territory, and efforts to develop geothermal energy and eco-tourism as sustainable economic alternatives.

sub_clusters.name: Kalinago Territory Preservation and Cultural Revival
sub_clusters.description: The Carib Territory (officially renamed Kalinago Territory in 2015) remains one of the last indigenous reserves in the Caribbean, home to approximately 3,000 Kalinago people. Efforts to preserve their language, traditions, and land rights continue alongside eco-tourism development.

sub_clusters.name: Hurricane Maria Devastation and Resilience
sub_clusters.description: Category 5 Hurricane Maria struck Dominica on September 18, 2017, causing catastrophic destruction — 90% of buildings were damaged or destroyed, all crops lost, and the island was largely cut off from communication. Prime Minister Roosevelt Skerrit declared Dominica had been 'wiped out.' The government launched an ambitious plan to become the world's first climate-resilient nation.

sub_clusters.name: Geothermal Energy and Sustainable Development
sub_clusters.description: Dominica's volcanic geology, including the famous Boiling Lake (the second-largest hot spring in the world), provides significant geothermal energy potential. The government has pursued geothermal development to achieve energy independence and position Dominica as a leader in sustainable development among small island states.
